did_you_know.text: Did you know? The chapter opens with the title “A psalm of David, to bring to remembrance.” The title itself emphasizes that the psalm is a prayer that brings the worshiper’s condition before the Lord.
Did you know? The psalmist turns to the Lord and asks Him not to rebuke him in anger or discipline him in wrath. Thus, his prayer begins with a plea for mercy, even before he describes his condition.

Did you know? The description of suffering uses images of arrows and a heavy hand: “Your arrows have pierced me” and “Your hand has pressed down on me.” These images express the severity of the affliction as the psalmist experiences it.

Did you know? The psalmist describes his suffering both physically and emotionally: there is no “soundness” in his flesh and no “peace” in his bones. He connects his condition with the Lord’s anger and with his own sin.
Did you know? The chapter portrays iniquity as a heavy burden: “Like a heavy load, they are too heavy for me.” The image emphasizes that the psalmist’s sins weigh on him beyond his ability to bear.

Did you know? The psalmist describes his wounds in stark terms: they “fester and stink,” and he attributes their condition to his “folly.” The description of illness is combined here with a personal acknowledgment of guilt.

Did you know? Despite his weakness, the psalmist declares that nothing is hidden from the Lord: “All my longings” and “my sighing” are before Him. In other words, the Lord knows both his innermost desire and his groaning.

Did you know? The illness isolates the psalmist socially: his loved ones, friends, and relatives stand at a distance. Meanwhile, those seeking his harm take advantage of his condition and speak of “mischief” and deceit.

Did you know? In the face of his enemies, the psalmist chooses not to respond; he compares himself to a deaf person and one who cannot speak. His silence is presented as part of his weakness, but it is also connected to his faith that the Lord will answer on his behalf.

Did you know? Near the end of his description of suffering, the psalmist says explicitly, “I will confess my iniquity” and “I am anxious because of my sin.” This is a direct confession, making clear that the psalm is not merely a request to be rescued from enemies but also an honest reckoning with sin.
